The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Existing detection methods typically require external knowledge bases, model ne-tuning, or cloud API access, limiting applicability in local inference contexts.
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Methods: We evaluate the Kerimov–Alekberli (K–A) information-geometric framework as a real-time, inference-time hallucination detector across six open-source LLMs deployed locally on Apple M5 Silicon via Ollama v0.23.2 (Q4_K_M quantisation).
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: The K–A framework monitors the KL divergence between consecutive output distributions relative to a Fisher Information Metric (FIM)-derived threshold (τ = 0.065), triggering First-Passage Time (FPT) alarms when generation departs from the stable Riemannian output manifold.
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: We evaluate 120 responses (6 models × 20 questions) drawn from three established benchmarks: HaluEval (14 questions; categories: Fact, Confuse, Date, Num, Trap), FEVER (4 questions; adversarial fact verification), and SimpleQA (2 questions; precise factual recall).
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: All questions are classified as difficulty level Hard, targeting known LLM failure modes including o-by-one numerical errors, geographical traps, and disputed-attribution confounds.
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Results: The K–A framework achieves a session hallucination detection rate of 90.9% (20/22 hallucinated responses correctly flagged) with zero false positives on correct responses (0/98).
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Model-level hallucination rates vary dramatically: deepseekr1:latest (Qwen3 CoT architecture, 5.2GB) exhibits a 95% hallucination rate (19/20 questions) with 100% K–A detection; gemma3:27b (Gemma3, 17.4GB) and gemma3:latest (4.3B, 3.3GB) achieve 0% hallucination.
The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-Source Large Language Models via the Kerimov–Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Two K–A false negatives involve con dent factual errors below the KL threshold.
